‘WALANG LUGAR SA LIPUNAN ANG MGA BASTOS!’

Nagsagawa ng protest march ang World March of Women-Pilipinas kasama ang ilan pang grupo gaya ng Women's Legal and Human Rights Bureau mula Philippine Children’s Medical Center hanggang sa Office of the Ombudsman ngayong Biyernes, Marso 6.

Nagsampa ng reklamo ang mga grupo laban kay Quezon City 4th District Rep. Bong Suntay sa umano’y paglabag nito sa Safe Spaces Act, the Magna Carta of Women, at Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees. 

Ito ay dahil sa ‘nag-init’ statement ni Suntay tungkol sa aktres at TV host na si Anne Curtis na anila’y “sexist” at “inappropriate.”

“Acts of sexual violence and sexist behavior against women and girls continue to be normalized, as though they are an inevitable part of women’s daily lives. 
We refuse to accept this reality,” giit pa ng Women's Legal and Human Rights Bureau sa isang Facebook statement. (via Bea Tanierla)

Photo courtesy: Women's Legal and Human Rights Bureau/Facebook

data.raw_text:
ICYMI O/N (tgif hagw!!)

Note: No ICYMIs until next Thursday

The Iran war continues, with transit remaining halted via Hormuz, as oil prices (CL +1.5%) drift back towards highs with the US admin reportedly hesitant to tap the SPR, while reports suggest the admin is also not going to get involved in oil futures trading (as some had suggested). The US providing temporary waivers for India to buy Russian oil has had limited impact on futures, meanwhile Qatar is warning of $150/bbl oil. Stocks have started to move lower (ES -0.2%, NQ -0.2%, RTY -0.1%) as the energy rip extends, with Europe cash indices paring intial strength (ES50 +0.3%, DAX +0.4%, CAC 40 +0.3%). It was a mixed risk tone in Asia (HSI +1.7%, NKY +0.6%, KOSPI flat, TAIEX -0.2%), where the Hang Seng outperformed with China tech leading on the back of WSJ reports Thursday about China being expected to push the US for a loosening of U.S. export restrictions on high-tech components. The Dollar is starting to firm again (DXY +0.1%) as yields also start to climb (US 10yy +2.7bps) with particular pressure in UK fixed income again (UK 10yy +6bps, UK 2yy +9bps) as BoE pricing sees a more noted unwind. Gold (+0.3%) and Silver (+1.6%) holding on to tentative gains. Aside from Iran, attention now on the US jobs report. A faltering jobs market would be a harder problem for the Fed to address in the backdrop of a global supply shock.
  
IRAN:

The Trump administration is ruling out deploying the Treasury Department to trade oil futures for now, according to a Bloomberg source. Officials have discussed getting the Treasury Department involved in selling and buying energy futures but believe the agency’s ability to meaningfully affect the market is limited given balooning activity in the market. Source also says admin is hesitant to tap SPR right away. (BBG)

The US has cleared the way for India to temporarily increase its purchases of Russian oil. “This deliberately short-term measure will not provide significant financial benefit to the Russian government as it only authorizes transactions involving oil already stranded at sea”, Treasury Sec Bessent announced. (BBG)

Indian refiners are moving quickly to buy Russian oil, with million of barrels floating in Asian waters offering a quick fix to a Middle East supply crunch after the US relaxed restrictions on the trade. More than 10mln bbls of Russian crude have already been bought, according to Bloomberg sources. Much of that may have been purchased even before the one-month waiver announced late Thursday in Washington. (BBG)

Trump calls US ground invasion in Iran ‘waste of time,’ regime ‘lost everything they can lose’. (NY Post)

Qatar Energy Minister al-Kaabi cautioned to the FT that the Middle East conflict could cause all Gulf energy producers to have to shut production within weeks, increasing oil to USD 150/bbl.  Adds, even if the conflict ended immediately, it would take weeks or months for Qatar to return to its usual delivery cycle. (FT)

Israel on Friday said it had started a "broad-scale" wave of attacks against infrastructure targets in Tehran, as Gulf cities came under renewed bombardment by Iran. (RTRS)

Iran launched an overnight drone attack on the U.S. Al Udied airbase in Qatar, the biggest U.S. base in the Middle East, Qatari officials said. There were no reported casualties. (RTRS)

The IRGC said Iranian forces had targeted the Ramat David airbase and a radar site in Israel, the Al-Adiri camp in Kuwait where U.S. forces are stationed, and a drone attack on a base hosting U.S. troops in Erbil, Iraq. A Guards spokesperson said new initiatives and weapons would soon be deployed to confront Israeli and U.S. aggression, without giving details. (RTRS)

The UAE is weighing freezing billions of dollars of Iranian assets held in the Gulf state, according to WSJ sources, a move that could sever one of Tehran’s most important economic lifelines. Emirati officials have privately warned Iran. (WSJ)

There’s “not a ton of confidence” that US security measures to protect oil and gas tankers in the Strait of Hormuz will resolve the current situation, according to Goldman Sachs Group Inc. Goldman says Brent prices could rise above $100 a barrel if disruptions in the strait extend to five weeks. (BBG)

Fuel oil traders in Asia are struggling to secure alternative ​supply as the Iran war curtails shipments from key Middle Eastern suppliers through the Strait of Hormuz, prompting them to look to ‌the West for replacement cargoes. "Everyone is struggling to find oil for the second half of March. Tankers are too expensive and arbitrage to Singapore is closed," a trader based in Singapore said to Reuters. (RTRS)

'Tehran Is Fighting With Jets That Date Back to the Vietnam War' WSJ article notes Iran’s air force is badly outdated, leaving it badly overmatched by modern Israeli and U.S. jets, leading Iran to lean more heavily into missiles and drones. (WSJ)

Gulf states could start to review their overseas investments and future commitments as they consider options to ease the pressure on their budgets following the U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran, the Financial Times reported. (FT)

The rapid expansion of American-owned data centres in the Middle East has opened up a new front for Iran’s retaliation against the US, complicating Gulf ambitions to build multibillion-dollar AI facilities in the region. (FT)

Emirates and Etihad Airways were resuming limited flight schedules to key global cities from their United Arab Emirates hubs on Friday, though the threat of missile fire piled pressure on airlines as they scramble to accommodate travellers. (RTRS)

Why oil at $200 a barrel is no longer unthinkable. (FT) 

Qatar is offering at least two liquefied natural gas tankers that it controls for lease, as the country’s massive export facility in the Persian Gulf remains shut due to the ongoing war in the Middle East. (BBG)

A 10% increase in energy prices that persists for a year would push global inflation up by 40 basis points and slow economic growth by 0.1-0.2%, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said. (BBG)

MACRO:

A U.S. judge will meet behind closed doors with government lawyers on Friday seeking to hammer out a process to refund up to $175 billion in illegally collected tariffs, a meeting a court official described as a "settlement conference." (RTRS)

U.S. job growth likely cooled in February, with hiring in the healthcare sector expected to return to normal trends after an outsized increase in January, but the unemployment rate is anticipated to have remained steady at 4.3%. (RTRS)

'Long-Trusted Haven Trades Are Failing as Gold, Treasuries Fall' BBG article highlights traditional safe havens — Treasuries, the yen, the Swiss franc, and gold — have offered investors no refuge this week. (BBG)

'How War in Iran Is Colliding With Trump’s Economic Priorities' WSJ artile notes the war with Iran is causing domestic economic challenges for President Trump, including rising gasoline prices and market instability, ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. (WSJ)

'Tariffs Are Lower and Businesses Are Racing to Take Advantage' WSJ article notes businesses hit by shifting U.S. tariffs are rushing to take advantage of a court-driven drop in rates by speeding up shipments, boosting production and pursuing refunds. (WSJ)

The Michigan Republican who chairs the Congressional Select Committee on China urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to closely scrutinize any expansion of US market access for Chinese manufacturers of cars, batteries and vehicle technology. (BBG)

The SEC on Thursday moved to dismiss a civil fraud lawsuit it had filed against crypto billionaire Justin Sun, who became a major investor in President Trump’s crypto projects as he pursued leniency from U.S. law enforcers. (WSJ)

Japan will coordinate with overseas authorities and stands ready to take action against market volatility stemming from the Middle East conflict, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Friday, issuing a fresh warning against sharp yen falls. BoJ Deputy Governor Himino also said the bank will be vigilant to yen moves. (RTRS)

The Bank of Japan is likely to hold off on raising interest rates until June or July, as the conflict in the Middle East shows few signs of easing and is seen keeping markets on edge, its former top economist Seisaku Kameda said on Friday. (RTRS)

There is still a 50% chance the Bank of Japan will raise its benchmark rate next month after a hold in March even after the conflict in Iran generated new uncertainties, according to Eiji Maeda, a former BOJ executive director who oversaw monetary policy. (BBG)

China will expand imports of advanced tech equipment and key parts, as well as high-quality consumer goods, Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao says at a National People’s Congress briefing. (BBG)

China’s effort to pivot its economy toward consumer spending will take a long time, according to a central bank adviser, even as Beijing adopts a softer growth target to signal a greater focus on rebalancing its growth drivers. (BBG)

Yuan financing has never been as popular as it is now, with more countries and foreign companies tapping the market, in a sign that China’s ambition to internationalize its currency is bearing fruit. (BBG)

US investors are increasingly asking Asian fund managers to carve out special vehicles so they can invest in the region without falling foul of American investment restrictions on Chinese technology. (FT)

Hong Kong’s economic growth for this year is expected to be higher than previously forecast, supported by improving financial activity and expansionary measures in the government’s Feb. 25 budget, according to the median estimate in a Bloomberg survey conducted March 2-5. (BBG)

European electricity prices are swinging wildly from daytime to evening as the Iran war’s disruption to gas supplies accentuates growing volatility in Europe’s power markets amid the rise of renewables. (FT)

ECB's Sleijpen said the surge in energy prices this week is not yet enough to move the bank's policy from what is currently a "good place" and the bank can in any case tolerate a small overshoot of its inflation target. (RTRS)

UK house prices rose in February at the fastest annual pace since October, data from mortgage lender Halifax showed on Friday, but concerns about a rise in inflation may temper the outlook for interest rates. (RTRS)

Poland will likely abstain from interest-rate cuts for as long as the armed conflict in Iran lasts, according to policymaker Henryk Wnorowski. (BBG)

Support for New Zealand’s ruling National party has fallen to its lowest level in more than four years and Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is no longer voters’ preferred leader, polling showed on Friday. (RTRS)

South Korea's consumer inflation remained at a five-month low of 2.0% in February, holding at the central bank's target level for the second straight month as prices of fresh food items stabilized, government data showed on Friday. (RTRS)

The Asian Development Bank's chief economist said that if the Middle East conflict and closure of the Strait of Hormuz last only about a month, the impact on growth in developing Asia would be modest, with only a slight and temporary "downward blip" in annual GDP. (RTRS)

Wealthy Asians look to move Dubai assets closer to home on Iran war fears. (RTRS)

Vietnam's police-owned telecom operator Mobifone is in talks with Chinese tech firms over new contracts to build parts of its 5G network, according to Reuters sources, despite U.S. warnings of security risks following earlier deals. (RTRS)

Philippines Central Bank Warns Oil at $100 May Trigger Rate Hike. (BBG)

Turkey has spent $12 billion, equal to roughly 15% of its foreign-currency reserves, to keep the lira stable during a week of global market volatility triggered by the war in Iran. (BBG)

GEOPOLITICAL:

The United States and interim authorities in Venezuela have agreed to re-establish diplomatic and consular relations, the U.S. State Department said on Thursday, aiming to foster a peaceful transition to elect a new government in the South American country. (RTRS)

The European Union’s enlargement chief said the destabilized world requires new rules to accelerate Ukraine’s membership bid, confirming the country won’t be able to join by its 2027 goal under the current process. (BBG)

Hong Kong conglomerate CK Hutchison on Friday said it has escalated its legal fight with Panama after the government seized its port operations, filing new treaty‑based claims and challenging the decree behind the takeover. (RTRS)

South Korea’s Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said Seoul is in talks with United States Forces Korea about the possible redeployment of weapons including Patriot air-defense systems, as Washington’s conflict with Iran escalates. (BBG)

EQUITIES:

SoftBank Group Corp. is seeking a loan of as much as $40 billion to mostly help finance its investment in US tech giant OpenAI, according to Bloomberg sources, in what would be its largest-ever borrowing denominated solely in dollars. (BBG)

Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei has apologized for a leaked memo in which he questioned the Trump administration’s motives for declaring his artificial-intelligence company a supply-chain risk and severing its government relationships. (WSJ)

Anthropic has said the Pentagon’s designation of the AI lab as a supply chain risk will not affect the “vast majority” of its customers as it vowed to fight the measure in court. (FT)

Canadian lawmakers say OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman pledged in conversations to strengthen protocols on notifying police over potentially harmful interactions with the company’s ChatGPT chatbot, and to issue an apology to the town reeling from a deadly school shooting. (WSJ)

DigiTimes article notes Intel’s EMIB gains traction as CoWoS alternative, reviving IC substrate investment. (DigiTimes via @jukan05)

China has approved Pfizer's GLP-1 treatment Xianweiying for long-term weight management in overweight or obese adults, the U.S. drugmaker said on WeChat on Friday, boosting competition in a market analysts expect to be worth billions of dollars. (RTRS)

Costco Wholesale Corp.’s quarterly profit rose more than expected, showing the club chain is capitalizing on an extended period of sales growth. (BBG)

Gap’s latest results were dented by more struggles at its Athleta brand, which posted another quarter of lower sales. (WSJ)

Nike expects to record a charge of $300 million related to cost-cutting efforts, including job eliminations. (WSJ)

Toyota supplier Denso is in talks to acquire shares of chipmaker Rohm in a potential $8.3-billion deal that will expand the auto parts maker's control over power management chips used in EVs and data centres. (RTRS)

Deutsche Lufthansa reported 2025 results slightly above average expectations due to lower costs and an increase in passengers. (WSJ)

Nexperia's Chinese subsidiary said on Friday most of the company's operations in China have resumed after being "significantly" disrupted following Nexperia's mass disabling of office accounts for all employees in the country. (RTRS)
